title: The Name on the hard road
word: The Name on the hard road
hook: the Name helps on the long road where all else fails (Sukhmani 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the door no family can pass, and your line: the name goes too. Did you tell someone who goes with them? Today, the road on the other side of that door. Day four hundred forty-four.

Before cars and highways, a long journey in Punjab meant walking. Days on dusty roads between towns, with no signposts you could trust and no inn guaranteed. Travelers packed a tosaa, a bundle of provisions: dry bread, roasted chickpeas, a little jaggery, wrapped in cloth. Without it you didn't leave. Sukhmani's second ashtpadi knows that world. It takes the traveler's bundle, the dark road, the burning sun, the stranger's town, and asks what you'd want with you on the hardest road of all.
screen: `A LONG ROAD ON FOOT.` → `A TOSAA: BREAD WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `WHAT DO YOU TAKE ON THE HARDEST ROAD?`

segments.voice: The stanza is a string of journeys, each with its own danger, and each answered by the Name. In paraphrase: on the road whose miles cannot be counted, the Name of God is your provisions there. On the road of utter darkness, the Name of God is the light with you. On the road where no one knows you, the Name of God is there to recognize you. Where the heat is fierce and the sun burns, the Name of God is your shade. Where thirst torments you, the Name of God rains down like nectar. Count the dangers. Distance. Darkness. Being a stranger. Heat. Thirst. Those are the five fears of any traveler on foot, and every one of them gets an answer. The word for provisions is tosaa, the bundle of food from the hook. So the Name is food when the road is too long, light when it's dark, a familiar face in a town of strangers, shade at noon, water when you're parched. Many Sikhs read this stanza as the journey after death, the road the previous stanza began. But they also hear it in life. A long illness has miles that can't be counted. Depression can be a road of utter darkness. Moving to a new country is a town where no one knows your name. The stanza doesn't say the road will be shortened. It doesn't promise you can skip it. It promises company on it, and provisions for it.
screen: `DISTANCE: THE NAME IS YOUR FOOD.` · `DARKNESS: THE NAME IS YOUR LIGHT.` · `A STRANGE TOWN: THE NAME KNOWS YOU.` · `HEAT AND THIRST: SHADE AND RAIN.` · then, large: `COMPANY ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry one line into a hard task. Think of one hard thing ahead of you today or this week, a long shift, a difficult call, a stretch of caring for someone. Pick the one image from the stanza that fits it best: food for the long road, light in the dark, a known face among strangers, shade, rain. Say that image to yourself slowly, three times. If you pray, add Waheguru. Then breathe with it, and picture yourself walking into the task carrying it like a bundle in cloth. The bell holds the time.
The Name on the hard road. In Sukhmani's second ashtpadi, the Name is food on the endless road, light in the dark, a friend among strangers, shade in the heat, rain in the thirst.
screen: `THE NAME ON THE HARD ROAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: company on the road. When your hard task begins today, remember the image you packed, and take it out once in the middle. Day four hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this stanza within the second ashtpadi, and many return to it during long illnesses, journeys and other hard stretches of life.

fork.setup: you're on a road so long its miles can't be counted, and your bundle of food is gone. what does the stanza say is with you?
options: the Name of God as your provisions.
fork.reveal: on the road whose miles cannot be counted, the Name of God is your provisions, your tosaa, there.

original.note: Gurmukhi: tosaa, a traveler's provisions; the stanza says the Name is your tosaa on the endless road.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Name on the hard road is a comforting phrase.
what it means: on every danger of the journey, distance, darkness, strangeness, heat, thirst, the Name is the provision and the companion.
what a scholar hears: the pauri uses the traveler's vocabulary of its day, kos (a measure of distance) and tosaa (provisions), and is often read of the soul's path after death.

notes: Pauri paraphrased (endless road / provisions; utter darkness / light; no one knows you / recognizes you; heat / shade; thirst / nectar rain). Confirm these lines and that they sit in one pauri of ashtpadi 2 (likely pauri 2).
Kos as a measure of distance in the trapdoor: confirm the pauri uses kosaa.
Travel provisions in the hook (dry bread, roasted chickpeas, jaggery) are illustrative; confirm acceptable.
